docs.title: InferScale: One ML Inference Service on Three Clouds with cmx vm
docs.text: Course: COMP 488 – Cloud Computing, DevOps, and AI Team Members - Khaja Shabbir Ahmed – Cloud / DevOps Engineer (solo project) Contact kahmed5@luc.edu Instructor Gregor von Laszewski Repository https://github.com/cloudmesh-ai-luc/shabbir04 Date Sep. 22, 2026

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
Problem. The same AI service often has to run on more than one cloud, but every cloud has its own way to create VMs, give them a public IP and clean them up. That makes deployments hard to repeat and clouds hard to compare fairly.

What InferScale does. InferScale is a small two-tier machine-learning service: a web frontend (nginx and a small HTML/JavaScript page) in front of a backend that serves a sentiment-analysis model (DistilBERT) through a FastAPI REST API. Each tier is its own Docker container, and the same two containers run on three clouds: Multipass on my laptop (local), Chameleon KVM@TACC (OpenStack) and AWS EC2 (public cloud). All VMs are created, reached and deleted with one tool, cmx vm from the class project cloudmesh-ai-vm, which I also contribute to. One deploy script runs the same steps on every cloud, and a load test measures how each cloud performs. On top of plain predictions, InferScale has three features: an AI review filter, live monitoring with alerts of all three clouds (Prometheus and Grafana), and multi-cloud failover.

Result. A repeatable, automated workflow and a side-by-side comparison of deployment time, response time and cost on the three clouds. Where cmx vm falls short for this workflow, I fix it in small pull requests (for example the cmx vm ip command).

docs.title: 2. Cloud Computing, DevOps, and AI
docs.text: Area How InferScale addresses it Cloud Computing Runs the same service as VMs (IaaS) on three different kinds of cloud: a local hypervisor, an OpenStack research cloud and a public cloud. Each VM runs a two-tier application: a public web frontend in front of a private model backend. Uses each cloud's networking (local IP, floating IP, public IP), security groups, Chameleon leases, and compares cost. cmx vm hides the differences behind one command line. Feature: multi-cloud failover. When one cloud is down, requests go to the next cloud. DevOps GitHub flow (branches, pull requests, issues), automated tests and Docker builds with GitHub Actions, a container registry, one deploy script for all clouds, a smoke test after every deployment, and clean-up so nothing keeps running. Feature: live monitoring with alerts. Every VM reports its requests, errors and response time at /metrics. Prometheus collects them from all three clouds, Grafana shows them on one dashboard, and an alert fires when a cloud stops answering or has too many errors. AI The workload is an AI model: DistilBERT sentiment analysis served for inference on CPU. The project measures how fast that model answers on each cloud. Feature: review filter. The model returns only the reviews with a chosen label (for example, negative) that it is confident about.

docs.title: 3. Objectives & Success Criteria
docs.text: # Objective Success criterion 1 Package the frontend and backend tiers as Docker images /health and /predict pass the tests; the web page shows a prediction; CI builds both images 2 Run the service on three clouds using cmx vm for all VM management /predict answers on Multipass, Chameleon and AWS 3 Automate the deployment ./deploy.sh <cloud> goes from no VM to a working service with one command 4 Measure and compare the clouds A results table with deploy time, latency (p50/p95), success rate and cost per cloud 5 Improve cmx vm where the project needs it Small, reviewed pull requests to cloudmesh-ai-vm 6 AI review filter /filter returns only the reviews with the chosen label and a score at or above the threshold 7 Live monitoring with alerts One Grafana dashboard shows requests, errors and response time for all three clouds, updated every 5 seconds; an alert fires when a cloud stops answering 8 Multi-cloud failover With one cloud's VM deleted during a test run, requests still succeed through the other clouds

docs.title: 4. Scope
docs.text: In scope Out of scope Two tiers: web frontend (nginx + HTML/JavaScript) and backend (FastAPI + DistilBERT), each in its own Docker image Training or fine-tuning models Three clouds: Multipass, Chameleon KVM@TACC, AWS EC2 Kubernetes and autoscaling (dropped to keep the project simple) Deploy script built on cmx vm GPUs CI with GitHub Actions High availability and 24/7 monitoring (monitoring runs only during my sessions) Load test and comparison of the three clouds Other public clouds (Azure, GCP) Small fixes to cmx vm A load balancer in front of the clouds (failover is done in the client) Three features: review filter, live monitoring with alerts, multi-cloud failover Sending alerts by email or chat (alerts are shown in Prometheus and Grafana) User logins and frontend frameworks such as React

docs.title: 5.2 Three Clouds and cmx vm
docs.text:
Why these three. Multipass is free and fast for development. Chameleon KVM@TACC is the class OpenStack cloud (project CH-817419). AWS is the most widely used public cloud, and new accounts get Free plan credits.

Local OpenStack Public Cloud Multipass on my Mac Chameleon KVM@TACC AWS EC2 cmx vm provider multipass chameleon aws VM size 1 vCPU, 2 GB (set in ~/.config/cloudmesh/clouds.yaml) m1.small (1 vCPU, 2 GB) t3.small (2 vCPU, 2 GB) OS image Ubuntu 22.04 CC-Ubuntu22.04 Ubuntu 22.04 How the service is reached The VM's local IP Floating IP The instance's public IP Port 80 (frontend tier) Open by default Rule added with cmx vm security-group Rule in the instance's security group Special step None cmx vm start creates a lease; end the lease after cmx vm delete Delete the instance after every session Status cmx vm VM lifecycle tested start, list, ip assign, delete tested (Oct 14) Account and credentials not set up yet

The steps deploy.sh runs on every cloud:

cmx vm cloud set chameleon                 # multipass | chameleon | aws
cmx vm start inferscale                    # Chameleon: also creates a lease (--duration 2h)
cmx vm list                                # shows the VM and its IP
cmx vm run inferscale "curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo sh"
cmx vm run inferscale "sudo docker network create inferscale && \
  sudo docker run -d --name api --network inferscale ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-api:latest && \
  sudo docker run -d --name web --network inferscale -p 80:80 ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-web:latest"
curl http://<ip>/api/health                # smoke test through the frontend tier
locust -f loadtest.py --headless -u 10 -r 2 -t 60s --host http://<ip>
cmx vm delete inferscale                   # Chameleon: then delete the lease

Only the web container publishes a port (-p 80:80). The api container has no public port; web reaches it by name (api:8000) on the private Docker network inferscale.

On Chameleon a VM can also be started without an IP (cmx vm start inferscale --ip no) and get one later with cmx vm ip assign inferscale.

Multi-cloud failover. deploy.sh writes each cloud's IP into a small config file. client.py tries the clouds in order, so the service keeps answering when one cloud is down:

import requests

CLOUDS = ["http://<aws-ip>/api", "http://<chameleon-ip>/api", "http://<multipass-ip>/api"]

def predict(text):
    for url in CLOUDS:
        try:
            return requests.post(f"{url}/predict", json={"text": text}, timeout=3).json()
        except requests.RequestException:
            continue  # this cloud is down, try the next one
    raise RuntimeError("all clouds are down")

The demo: run requests through client.py, delete the AWS VM with cmx vm delete, and the requests keep working through Chameleon.

docs.title: 5.3 DevOps Pipeline
docs.text:
Stage Tool What it does Source GitHub One branch per change, pull requests, issues Test pytest (GitHub Actions) Tests /health and /predict on every push Build Docker (GitHub Actions) Builds the two images (inferscale-web, inferscale-api) and pushes them to GitHub Container Registry Deploy deploy.sh + cmx vm Creates the VM and starts both containers on the chosen cloud Verify curl /api/health, Locust Checks the service through the frontend tier, then measures latency Monitor Prometheus + Grafana Shows live requests, errors and response time for all three clouds, and raises an alert when a cloud is down or has too many errors Clean up cmx vm delete Removes the VM (and the Chameleon lease) after each session

The Python environment is a venv with pip, not conda, which keeps the VMs and containers clean.

Live monitoring with alerts. Prometheus and Grafana run in Docker on my laptop (docker compose up). deploy.sh writes each cloud's IP into targets.json, and Prometheus reads the file again when it changes. Prometheus collects /api/metrics through the frontend tier of every cloud every 5 seconds and checks two alert rules:

# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: inferscale
    scrape_interval: 5s
    metrics_path: /api/metrics   # nginx forwards it to the backend
    file_sd_configs:
      - files: [targets.json]    # one entry per cloud, e.g. {"targets": ["<aws-ip>:80"], "labels": {"cloud": "aws"}}
rule_files: [alerts.yml]

# alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: inferscale
    rules:
      - alert: CloudDown          # a cloud does not answer for 1 minute
        expr: up{job="inferscale"} == 0
        for: 1m
      - alert: HighErrorRate      # more than 5 % of requests fail for 1 minute
        expr: sum by (cloud) (rate(http_requests_total{status="5xx"}[1m]))
              / sum by (cloud) (rate(http_requests_total[1m])) > 0.05
        for: 1m

The Grafana dashboard has one line per cloud for requests per second, errors and p95 response time, and a panel that lists the alerts that are firing.

docs.title: 5.4 Frontend Tier
docs.text:
InferScale has two tiers. Each runs in its own container on the same VM:

Frontend tier Backend tier Container web: nginx + one HTML/JavaScript page api: FastAPI + DistilBERT Image ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-web ghcr.io/shabbir04/inferscale-api Job Shows the web page and forwards every /api/... request to the backend Runs the model and answers /health, /predict, /filter, /metrics Port 80, the only public port 8000, only on the internal Docker network 
flowchart LR
    U[Browser, client.py,<br/>Locust, Prometheus] -->|HTTP :80| WEB
    subgraph VM[One VM on each cloud]
        WEB[web container<br/>nginx + web page] -->|"/api/ → api:8000 (internal network)"| API[api container<br/>FastAPI + DistilBERT]
    end

The page has two parts: type one review and press Analyze to see its label and score, or paste several reviews and press Filter to see only the confident ones with the chosen label. nginx serves the page and passes API calls to the backend:

# nginx.conf in the web image
server {
    listen 80;
    location /     { root /usr/share/nginx/html; }   # the web page
    location /api/ { proxy_pass http://api:8000/; }  # forward to the backend tier
}

The page calls the backend only through nginx, so the browser never talks to the model container directly:

async function analyze() {
  const text = document.getElementById("text").value;
  const r = await fetch("/api/predict", {method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json"},
                                         body: JSON.stringify({text})});
  const {label, score} = await r.json();
  document.getElementById("result").textContent = `${label} (${score.toFixed(2)})`;
}

The page and the API come from the same address, so no CORS setup is needed.

docs.title: 5.5 AI / Model Serving (Backend Tier)
docs.text:
The model is distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english. It is small enough to run on a CPU and fit in a 2 GB VM. The core of the service:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from prometheus_fastapi_instrumentator import Instrumentator
from transformers import pipeline

app = FastAPI()
Instrumentator().instrument(app).expose(app)   # adds GET /metrics
classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis",
                      model="distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.post("/predict")
def predict(item: dict):
    return classifier(item["text"])[0]   # e.g. {"label": "POSITIVE", "score": 0.99}

@app.post("/filter")
def filter_reviews(item: dict):
    # e.g. {"texts": [...], "label": "NEGATIVE", "min_score": 0.9} -> only the confident negative reviews
    label = item.get("label", "NEGATIVE")
    min_score = item.get("min_score", 0.9)
    results = classifier(item["texts"])
    return [{"text": t, **r} for t, r in zip(item["texts"], results)
            if r["label"] == label and r["score"] >= min_score]

/metrics comes from the prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator library. It counts every request with its status code and response time, in the format Prometheus reads.

docs.title: 5.6 Security
docs.text:
• Login to VMs only with SSH keys, no passwords.
  • Cloud credentials stay in ~/.config/ and are never committed to Git.
  • Only port 80 (the frontend tier) is open, and only during testing. The backend has no public port: it is reached only through nginx on the internal Docker network. Every VM is deleted after each session.
  • Prometheus and Grafana run only on my laptop, so their web pages are not open to the internet.
  • The test data is public example text, with no personal data.

docs.title: 8. Risk Management
docs.text: Risk Likelihood Impact Mitigation Chameleon has no free capacity ("No valid host was found") Medium Delay Retry at another time; keep sessions short A Chameleon lease keeps running after cmx vm delete High Uses allocation End the lease after every session An AWS instance is left running Low Cost Delete after every session; set a billing alert The model needs more memory than the VM has Medium Service crashes Use 2 GB VMs; add swap or use a smaller model Credentials leak Low High Keep them only in ~/.config/, never in Git The failover demo needs two or three clouds running at once Medium More cost and allocation Keep the demo under 30 minutes and delete everything right after

docs.title: 11. Issues
docs.text:
• AWS is not set up yet. I still need the account and credentials, and I have not tested whether the aws provider in cmx vm supports everything the deploy script needs (public IP, security group rule). If not, I open the port in the AWS console and report the gap.
  • Which Chameleon code to use. cmx vm has two versions for Chameleon: the dev2 branch and the feature/chameleon-native-chi branch. I need to know which one the project should build on.
  • Chameleon clean-up gaps. cmx vm delete does not end the lease, and releasing a floating IP fails because python-chi uses a compute call that KVM@TACC no longer supports, so IPs stay reserved.
  • Is 2 GB enough for DistilBERT plus Docker? If not, I add swap or use a smaller model.
  • The VMs are not identical (t3.small has 2 vCPUs, m1.small has 1), so the results note the differences instead of treating them as a perfectly fair comparison.
  • Failover is done in the client. It is the simplest way. A load balancer in front of the clouds would be more realistic, but it needs another VM. The cloud IPs also change with every deployment, so deploy.sh has to update the client's config file and Prometheus's targets.json each time.
